newsitem.title: USA: First Union seen raising financial targets.
newsitem.headline: First Union seen raising financial targets.

text.p: First Union Corp, the sixth largest U.S. banking company whose stock has been lagging some of its peers, is expected to raise financial targets Friday in its effort to whip up more enthusiasm on Wall Street.
Company executives are scheduled to brief analysts in a length session running most of the morning.
"What they will talk about is a raising of tneir financial targets," said Moshe Orenbuch, analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein Co. He declined to predict what the new targets might be.
A First Union spokesman declined comment.

First Union is expected to state new goals for return on equity (ROE) and return on assets (ROA) and an annual growth rate in earnings per share. In 1995, First Union had ROE of 16.69 percent and ROA of 1.21 percent. Net income in 1995 rose about nine percent from 1994. Results in 1996 have been hurt by merger-related restructuring charges, although First Union's earnings have been meeting analysts' expectations.

One disenchanted analyst is Nancy Bush of Brown Brothers Harriman. After the third-quarter earnings in mid-October, Bush lowered her rating to market perform/hold from outperform/buy. She cited "earnings quality" in the quarter.

Earnings per share for the first nine months of 1996 were down 4.2 percent to $3.69. The results have been impacted by a one-time charge for recapitalizing the Savings Association Insurance Fund (SASF) as well as merger expenses.

Bush said First Union has been talking about earning $7.00 per share in 1997, but she believes it will be "a pretty tough number to achieve." Her own estimate is $6.85 per share, up from an estimated $6.30 this year.
The analyst said a special concern is $1 billion in underperforming credit card assets.
Bush said that, while First Union at one time was going to sell the underperforming assets, a sale is no longer expected.
"There would be some haircut on selling these things that they just don't want to take," she said.

While some analysts make the point that credit cards are a relatively small operation at First Union, Bush said that, with low reserves, there is an earnings problem caused by the credit cards. "The issue is not 'how big is the portfolio?' it's 'how bad is the portfolio?'," she said. Her rating cut was "not a signal to push the panic button", but advice to look for "more interesting things out there."
First Union got a big boost this week from analyst Lawrence Cohn of PaineWebber Group Inc, who started research coverage with a buy rating.

The analyst said credit cards have never been a significant part of the consumer loan mix and have been only a small portion of the overall portfolio. He noted that on the commercial side, First Union has avoided large credit exposure to the cyclical construction and development area.
Nevertheless, Cohn and other analysts expect a rise in the loan loss provision in 1997. Cohn expects the provison to rise to about $580 million next year from $370 million this year.

Cohn said the appeal of First Union is its targeting of consumers and small and medium-size corporate customers. He said such business customers are more loyal and less price conscious than their larger counterparts and, when properly managed, the business offers the best growth prospects in an industry facing inherently slow growth.

Orenbuch said one question on the minds of analysts is whether or not First Union will change its planned acquisition of Keystone Investments Inc to a purchase accounting method from pooling accounting. Purchase accounting would permit share buybacks that would go over well on Wall Street.
